04 · Read & review

The transcript

0:00 / 0:00

Submit all six answers to unlock the transcript. You can then listen and read together.

Fiona Bell's email arrived with the first account of what was actually inside the folder labelled “Payment exceptions — 2011”. The records team had examined an introductory sheet defining the category. It was a guide to recordkeeping rather than a ledger of individual cases, and Fiona was careful about the distinction.

According to the sheet, a payment could be marked as an exception when supporting documents were missing, travel arrangements changed or a bank transfer was returned. The guide gave no totals. Nor had the team reconciled any entries with evidence of transfers eventually reaching students.

“A returned payment sounds serious,” Sarah said when Emma called.

“It could be,” Emma replied. “But a returned transfer might have been corrected and sent again. We need the later record, not just the first problem.”

They mapped the new information against Helen Ward's redacted decision letter. Helen's cousin had apparently been selected, subject to enrolment and travel checks. That notice still did not establish that an authorisation had been made, or that any money had been transferred.

Helen later responded to Emma's enquiry. Her cousin had not located a bank statement from 2011 and could not remember when, or even with confidence whether, a payment had arrived. Helen specifically asked the newsroom not to treat the missing paperwork as proof of non-payment. Emma recorded that limitation without trying to persuade the family to release more private records.

Another paragraph in the trust's guidance caught Emma's attention. When an exception was settled, administrators were instructed to enter a follow-up reference. In principle, a sequence of original and follow-up entries might establish whether a problem had been resolved. But Fiona had not yet determined whether those references survived or could be matched reliably.

Sarah proposed counting the outstanding cases. Emma agreed only conditionally: they would need to distinguish cases still unresolved in 2011 from files that were merely incomplete today. A missing follow-up document was not necessarily an unresolved transfer.

Then Fiona sent a brief update. In the preliminary material, staff had seen entries marked “manual approval”. No signatory, reason or associated bank transaction had yet been checked. The phrase might simply refer to a standard exception-handling process.

Emma thought again about the caller who had urged her to ask who approved the payments. The wording was suggestive, but anonymous instructions could not authenticate an accounting entry.

She wrote three questions: What required manual approval? Who was authorised to give it? What happened to the payment afterwards? Unlike the newspaper's disputed selection total, these questions could eventually be answered by records of a particular process.

For the moment, the trust had supplied definitions, not findings. Still, it had given Emma a sharper route through the numbers.
